idiom_name: trait Mapper[A, B] + given instances + extension method
implementation_notes: Scala 3 expresses the mapping as a typeclass: `trait Mapper[A, B] { def map(a: A): B }` with `given Mapper[UserDto, User] with ...` instances in the boundary package and an extension `extension [A](a: A) def to[B](using m: Mapper[A, B]): B = m.map(a)`, so call sites summon the conversion (`dto.to[User]`) and generic code can require `A: Mapper[*, User]` without naming concrete types. The rules live in the instances - one per pair - and the compiler refuses a conversion for which no instance is in scope, a stronger isolation than a mapper class provides. Use plain instances for total conversions and `Try`/`Either`-returning instances when parsing can fail.
pitfalls: Given resolution is scope-based: an instance that is not imported produces a confusing 'no instance found' error even though the mapping exists.
Two instances for the same pair in scope are an ambiguity error; keep exactly one per pair in a known package and never derive a generic fallback instance.
Implicit summoning hides the call: the conversion site reads as `.to[User]`, so stack traces and code search stop at the extension method, not at the instance.

variants.name: Companion-object conversion methods (classic form)
variants.idiom_name: object User { def fromDto(d: UserDto): User } / mapper object with toDto
variants.implementation_notes: The Scala 2 style - still common and entirely honest - puts the conversion in the target's companion object (`object User { def fromDto(d: UserDto): User = ... }`) or in a `UserMapper` object with `toDto`/`fromDto` methods: the classic Mapper structure in Scala syntax, with no typeclass machinery, and readable at every call site. Choose it when the pairs are few and fixed, when the call sites are not generic, or when the team prefers explicit names over implicit summoning; the typeclass pays off only when conversions must be discovered generically by library code or DSLs.
pitfalls: Companion-object methods create a compile-time dependency from the domain type to the DTO type - keep them in a mapper object in the boundary package when that dependency is unwanted.
Case-class construction is positional by accident: `User(d.id, d.name)` compiles when both fields are strings but swaps meaning, so always name the arguments.
A mapper object accumulating methods for many types becomes a god mapper; split per pair as soon as a second representation appears.
